title: math, random and statistics
intro: Three small modules cover most everyday number work. `math` has rounding helpers, square roots, π and safe float comparison. `random` picks, shuffles and generates values — and with a **seed** it repeats the same values every time, which makes programs testable. `statistics` gives mean, median, mode and spread.

questions.prompt: `random.Random(seed)` makes your own generator. Two generators with the same seed produce the same sequence.
questions.exampleCode:
import math, random, statistics

print(math.sqrt(81), math.ceil(2.1), math.floor(2.9))   # 9.0 3 2
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))                    # True

rng = random.Random(7)
print(rng.randint(1, 6), rng.choice(["red", "green"]))

print(statistics.mean([3, 5, 10]), statistics.median([3, 5, 10]))  # 6 5
questions.explanation: Run the example twice: the random values stay the same, because of the seed.

questions.hint: `floor` always goes *down*; `round` sends halves to the even number.
questions.explanation: `ceil` rounds up, `floor` rounds down (so −4.1 becomes −5), and `round(2.5)` is 2 because Python rounds halves to the nearest even number.

questions.prompt: Write `boxes_needed(items, per_box)` that returns how many boxes you need to pack every item. A part-full box still counts.
questions.starterCode:
def boxes_needed(items, per_box):
    return items // per_box

tests.name: exact
tests.code: assert boxes_needed(12, 6) == 2, '12 items, 6 per box: 2 boxes.'

tests.name: partial
tests.code: assert boxes_needed(13, 6) == 3 and boxes_needed(1, 6) == 1, 'Leftover items need one more box.'

tests.name: none
tests.code: assert boxes_needed(0, 6) == 0, 'No items need no boxes.'

questions.hint: `//` rounds down. You need to round up.
questions.explanation: `math.ceil(items / per_box)` rounds up, so leftovers get a box of their own.

questions.prompt: Write `distance(p, q)` that returns the straight-line distance between two points given as `(x, y)` tuples.

tests.name: float
tests.code:
import math as _m
assert _m.isclose(distance((1, 1), (2, 2)), 1.41421356, rel_tol=1e-6), 'From (1, 1) to (2, 2) is about 1.414.'

tests.name: negative
tests.code: assert distance((-1, -1), (2, 3)) == 5, 'It should work with negative coordinates.'

questions.hint: Pythagoras: √(dx² + dy²). `math.hypot(dx, dy)` does it in one call.
questions.explanation: `math.hypot` is clearer and more accurate than squaring and adding by hand.

questions.prompt: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False`. What's the right way to compare floats?
questions.hint: Floats are stored in binary and carry tiny errors.
questions.explanation: `math.isclose` allows a tiny tolerance. Rounding to whole numbers or comparing strings throws away real differences.

questions.prompt: `roll_dice(n, seed)` should give the **same** rolls every time it gets the same seed, so tests can rely on it. It ignores the seed. Fix it.
questions.solution:
import random

def roll_dice(n, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]

tests.name: shape
tests.code:
r = roll_dice(20, 1)
assert len(r) == 20 and all(1 <= x <= 6 for x in r), 'It should return n rolls from 1 to 6.'

tests.name: repeatable
tests.code: assert roll_dice(15, 42) == roll_dice(15, 42), 'The same seed should give the same rolls.'

tests.name: seed matters
tests.code: assert roll_dice(15, 1) != roll_dice(15, 2), 'Different seeds should give different rolls.'

questions.hint: Make a generator from the seed: `random.Random(seed)`.
questions.explanation: A local `random.Random(seed)` is repeatable and doesn't disturb the shared generator other code uses.

questions.prompt: For `scores = [72, 85, 91, 85, 64, 99, 78]`, use `statistics` to set `avg` (the mean), `mid` (the median) and `most_common` (the mode).
questions.solution:
import statistics

scores = [72, 85, 91, 85, 64, 99, 78]
avg = statistics.mean(scores)
mid = statistics.median(scores)
most_common = statistics.mode(scores)

tests.name: mean
tests.code: assert avg == 82, 'avg should be the mean, 82.'

tests.name: median
tests.code: assert mid == 85, 'mid should be the median, 85.'

tests.name: mode
tests.code: assert most_common == 85, 'most_common should be the mode, 85.'

questions.explanation: The median is the middle value once sorted — less affected by one unusually high or low score than the mean.

questions.prompt: Fill in the function that mixes a list into a random order, in place.
questions.hint: Like shuffling a deck of cards.
questions.explanation: `random.shuffle` changes the list itself and returns `None`, so don't write `deck = random.shuffle(deck)`.

questions.prompt: Write `pick_winners(names, k, seed)` that returns `k` **different** names chosen at random, repeatable for the same seed. Don't change `names`.

tests.name: winners
tests.code:
people = ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Caro', 'Dev', 'Eli', 'Fay']
w = pick_winners(people, 3, 5)
assert len(w) == 3 and len(set(w)) == 3 and set(w) <= set(people), 'Pick 3 different names from the list.'

tests.name: repeatable
tests.code:
people = ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Caro', 'Dev', 'Eli', 'Fay']
assert pick_winners(people, 2, 9) == pick_winners(people, 2, 9), 'The same seed should pick the same winners.'

tests.name: unchanged
tests.code:
people = ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Caro', 'Dev']
pick_winners(people, 2, 1)
assert people == ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Caro', 'Dev'], 'names should not be changed.'

questions.hint: `sample(list, k)` picks k different items without changing the list.
questions.explanation: `sample` never picks the same item twice; `choice` in a loop could.

questions.prompt: You need to generate a password-reset code. Which module should you use?
questions.explanation: `random` is fine for games and simulations, but someone could predict its output. `secrets` is made for security tokens.
